newsitem.title: USA: Arkansas pair settles SEC insider trading charges.
newsitem.headline: Arkansas pair settles SEC insider trading charges.

text.p: Two Arkansas men agreed to pay a total of $221,789 to settle charges they violated securities laws by trading on confidential information, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission said Tuesday.

The two Little Rock residents, David Schmidt, 38, and his father-in-law, Willard Whitehurst, 59, neither admitted nor denied allegations filed by the SEC in a civil complaint in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.
Schmidt agreed to pay $105,241.99 in alleged profits derived from insider trading, prejudgment interest of $23,332.96 and a civil penalty of $68,206.93.
Whitehurst agreed to turn over $4,240.62 in alleged gains from insider trading, prejudgment interest of $940.16 and a civil penalty of $19,826.56, the regulatory agency said.

In its complaint, SEC alleged that in September 1994 Whitehurst learned of merger negotiations between Mark IV Industries and Purolator Products Co during his employment with Dayco Products Inc, a subsidiary of Mark IV.

The complaint alleges that Whitehurst asked Schmidt to buy $10,000 worth of Puralotor's common stock and then tipped him off about the negotiations. Schmidt also recommended three other persons buy Purolator common stock, the SEC alleged.

Collectively, Whitehurst, Schmidt and the persons tipped off by Schmidt bought 15,173 Purolator common shares, the SEC alleged. After the announcement of the merger agreement, they sold or tendered their shares for a profit of $109,483, the commission said.

Purolator, based in Tulsa, Okla., was a manufacturer, distributor and marketer of filtration products and systems. Mark IV, based in Amherst, New York, makes power and fluid transfer products, transportation and professional audio.
Dayco Products is based in Miamisburg, Ohio.
